question: A programme manager connects her Gmail account to a private Claude project so she can draft client status updates using recent correspondence. She writes a draft inside that project and then sends it in an email to an external partner agency the programme works with. What is the greatest risk in this workflow?
options: A) The partner agency gains the same access to her mailbox the moment she sends the draft, because the connector automatically reaches everyone the email goes to.
B) Details from messages unrelated to the update can surface in the draft, and she carries them outside the organisation when she sends it.
C) Connecting her mailbox pulls every message into the project's knowledge base as if each one had been uploaded.
D) The mailbox connector stops working the moment she copies text out of the project chat into an email.
correct_answers: B) Details from messages unrelated to the update can surface in the draft, and she carries them outside the organisation when she sends it.
explanations: Wrong. A connector is authorised for her own account and enforced at the user level; sending an email to the partner agency does not extend that authorisation to them, and the project she is working in was never shared with the partner because connectors are only available in private projects.

Correct. Claude can surface anything it finds relevant while searching her mailbox, so material from messages that have nothing to do with the update can end up woven into the draft. Once she emails that draft to the partner agency, whatever slipped in leaves the organisation with it.
Wrong. Claude draws on a connected mailbox only when something in it is relevant to the request being handled, rather than importing every message wholesale into the project's knowledge base.
Wrong. The connector stays authorised on her account independently of what she does with the content it surfaces; copying text out of a project chat has no effect on the connection itself.
